source_quality.text_layer: partial; seven empty or near-empty text pages reconciled visually

task_reconstruction.summary: First design a non-destructive, low-cost, small-team measurement plan.
Check external consistency, age and reliability, repair, source, and short-heavy versus long-light use.

section_map.summary: Staircase Wear Analysis - Walking Through History joins the observable object, analytical action, and historical inference in one compact title.

The eight-paragraph summary advances from archaeological need through measurement, Delaunay volume, Archard traffic, movement distributions, age inference, repair and source checks, usage kurtosis, and sensitivity.
The introduction establishes archaeological value, behavior questions, a material-wear research gap, the choice of Archard wear, and the need for C14, weathering, and depth-estimation evidence.
The restatement first fixes a low-cost non-destructive measurement prerequisite and then enumerates eight outputs: traffic, direction, occupancy, consistency, age, repair, source, and usage regime.
Figure 1 turns the eight questions into a measurement-to-model-to-inference-to-evaluation workflow.
Table 1 binds physical, dating, weathering, and distribution symbols; five assumptions each expose a behavioral or material simplification and its rationale.
The measurement plan combines laser scanning, monocular depth with scale and gyroscope correction, isotope and mineral tests, microbial sampling, and 11 self-collected stair samples.
Delaunay triangles convert a surface integral to local volumes; adhesive and abrasive Archard relations feed daily traffic, while a grid-based Bayesian inversion couples usage time to wear volume.

Normal, truncated-normal, mixture, edge, and multi-person distributions connect longitudinal wear peaks to direction, side-by-side occupancy, and two-way traffic, with Monte Carlo illustrations and Shapiro-Wilk checks.
C14 decay handles wood; an exponential weathering model and three chemical indices handle stone; Bayesian likelihood, uncertainty propagation, and confidence intervals bound age estimates.
Age anomalies, external traffic intervals, material coefficients and composition, and wear-depth kurtosis extend the core models to repair, source, consistency, and usage-regime questions.
Normalized sensitivity compares Model I parameters, while Model II plots vary location, spread, and upward-share parameters.
The evaluation credits multimodal measurement and self-collected data, then limits claims because destructive factors, measurement accuracy, and random trajectories remain unresolved.
Fourteen references cover wear, scanning and depth estimation, isotope and microbial analysis, Delaunay geometry, stair biomechanics, dating, and chemical weathering.
The AI disclosure reproduces two code-oriented prompts and outputs for GLTF vertex binning, depth maps, and visualization; it is provenance only and is excluded from author-language counts.

contributions.summary: Combines physical, chemical, and biological evidence in one measurement plan.
Converts point-cloud wear into volume with Delaunay triangles.
Links Archard wear to daily traffic and a bounded Bayesian usage-time inversion.
Uses direction-specific distributions, edge adjustment, and multi-person superposition to infer movement patterns.
Combines C14, weathering indices, Bayesian inversion, and uncertainty propagation for age.
Extends age and wear outputs to repair, source, consistency, and usage-regime questions.

dependency_graph.summary: 3D scan, monocular depth, assays, and microbial samples supply geometry and material evidence.
Delaunay areas and mean depths supply total wear volume.
Wear volume, hardness, load, distance, and time supply traffic; the time prior and likelihood supply t_MAP.
Direction densities supply mixture, edge, Monte Carlo, and multi-person models.
C14 or weathering measurements supply age; propagated uncertainty supplies confidence intervals.
Local ages and wear quantities supply anomaly, consistency, source, and usage checks.

assumptions.summary: A single person's tread positions are normally distributed.
Each person spends the same time on every step.
All steps begin with the same material hardness and density.
Repairs reuse the original material and fill wear rather than rebuild the staircase.
Adhesive and abrasive Archard wear dominate the stair surface.
Direction can be represented by normal or truncated-normal wear along one axis.
Stone weathering follows exponential decay with a persistent microbial contribution.
Uncertainty inputs are independent for first-order propagation.

data_and_preprocessing.summary: Laser scan geometry and surface detail; use a ruler and gyroscope to correct monocular relative depth and camera angle.
Collect isotope ratios, mineral indices, microbial diversity, abundance, and weathering influence.
Use overhead photographs from four sites to create 11 wear-depth samples across cement, slate, marble, and granite.
Project point clouds, apply Delaunay triangulation, compute triangle area and mean depth, and sum volume.
Sort wear depths and calculate Shapiro-Wilk statistics after Monte Carlo pattern simulation.
Measure WI, PI, and LOI on low-traffic parts before constructing a rock-specific weathering score.

models.summary: Equation (1) preserves the surface-volume integral interface: Define continuous concave wear volume beneath the measured surface.
Equation (2) preserves the triangle area interface: Compute each Delaunay triangle area.
Equation (3) preserves the discrete volume sum interface: Aggregate local triangle volumes.
Equation (4) preserves the Archard adhesive wear interface: Relate adhesive wear volume to load, sliding distance, coefficient, and hardness.
Equation (5) preserves the abrasive coefficient interface: Approximate the abrasive geometric coefficient.
Equation (6) preserves the Archard abrasive wear interface: State the paper's simplified abrasive wear equation.
Equation (7) preserves the traffic distance interface: Convert daily traffic and usage time into cumulative friction distance.
Equation (8) preserves the daily traffic inversion interface: Infer daily foot traffic from total wear and duration.
Equation (9) preserves the usage-time prior interface: Bound prior usage time.
Equation (10) preserves the Gaussian likelihood interface: Score agreement between modeled and observed wear.
Equation (11) preserves the posterior kernel interface: Combine likelihood and prior.
Equation (12) preserves the MAP time interface: Select the most probable usage time on the grid.
Equation (13) preserves the MAP traffic interface: Recover traffic after time inversion.
Equation (14) preserves the upward truncated normal interface: Represent front-biased upward wear.
Equation (15) preserves the downward normal interface: Represent central or rear downward wear.
Equation (16) preserves the direction mixture interface: Mix upward and downward wear.
Equation (17) preserves the sample mean interface: Compute mean wear depth before testing normality.
Equation (18) preserves the test statistic interface: Test whether wear depths fit a normal or truncated-normal pattern.
Equation (19) preserves the mean interval interface: Bound the mean location after the distribution test.
Equation (20) preserves the edge-adjusted mixture interface: Increase predicted wear near stair edges.
Equation (21) preserves the side-by-side Gaussian sum interface: Superpose one wear peak per side-by-side walker.
Equation (22) preserves the C14 decay interface: Relate remaining carbon-14 to wood age.
Equation (23) preserves the C14 inversion interface: Invert the decay law for age.
Equation (24) preserves the weathering model interface: Represent time-dependent stone weathering plus persistent microbial effect.
Equation (25) preserves the weighted weathering indices interface: Combine three chemical indices for the weathering state.
Equation (26) preserves the weathering inversion interface: Infer stone construction age.
Equation (27) preserves the Gaussian age likelihood interface: Score an age hypothesis against the measured quantity.
Equation (28) preserves the propagation of uncertainty interface: Propagate independent measurement uncertainties into age.
Equation (29) preserves the 95 percent interval interface: Report a normal-approximation age interval.
Equation (30) preserves the sample-point set interface: Define locations used for repair-age comparison.
Equation (31) preserves the measurement set interface: Collect measured values at the selected points.
Equation (32) preserves the wood-age reuse interface: Compute local wood ages for anomaly comparison.
Equation (33) preserves the stone-age reuse interface: Compute local stone ages for anomaly comparison.
Equation (34) preserves the Z score interface: Flag locally inconsistent wear or age observations.
Equation (35) preserves the traffic reuse interface: Recompute traffic for comparison with known building use.
Equation (36) preserves the traffic interval interface: Define an acceptance interval for known traffic.
Equation (37) preserves the wood-year reuse interface: Compare inferred wood age with background information.
Equation (38) preserves the stone-year reuse interface: Compare inferred stone age with background information.
Equation (39) preserves the generic age interval interface: Generalize the age-consistency interval.
Equation (40) preserves the wear-coefficient inversion interface: Estimate a material wear coefficient for source comparison.
Equation (41) preserves the excess kurtosis interface: Separate peaked long-run wear from flatter short intense use.
Equation (42) preserves the normalized sensitivity interface: Compare relative output and parameter changes.
Triangulate projected points, compute cross-product areas and mean depths, then sum local volumes.
Evaluate the time prior and Gaussian wear likelihood on a bounded grid, select t_MAP, and compute daily traffic.
Sample direction and position patterns to produce single-up, single-down, and mixed surface heatmaps.
Place one normal peak per simultaneous walker and compare single-file, double-file, and two-way profiles.
Estimate local ages, compute local deviation scores, and flag abs(z)>2 as possible repair or renovation.

verification.summary: Apply the traffic equation to all 11 samples and compare estimated daily counts.
Compare Monte Carlo wear surfaces for upward, downward, and mixed movement.
Use Shapiro-Wilk and mean intervals to check a selected distribution family.
Compare projection curves from representative samples with predicted direction patterns.
Use local Z scores to flag possible renovation discontinuities.
Compare inferred traffic, age, coefficient, and composition with available background data.
Perturb Model I and Model II parameters in sensitivity plots.

results_trace.summary: The source classifies 11 samples as slight, moderate, or severe from collected photographs.
Table 3 reports inferred daily traffic from about 1215 to 8391 people per day under source assumptions.
Three projection curves are labeled mixed, mostly downward, and mostly upward.
Single, double, overlapping two-way, and separated two-way patterns are distinguished qualitatively.
Absolute Z score above 2 is used as a repair or renovation flag.
The paper maps high versus low kurtosis to long-light versus short-heavy use and ranks Model I sensitivities.

writing_logic.summary: Summary chain: need -> measurement -> volume -> Model I -> Model II -> age -> repairs/source/usage -> sensitivity.
Introduction chain: archaeological observable -> behavior questions -> research gap -> wear taxonomy -> method choices -> eight tasks.
Notation and assumption/reason pairs prepare variables and boundaries before acquisition.
Model I prose uses continuous target -> discrete geometry -> physical law -> inversion -> sample table.
Model II prose uses force contrast -> distribution family -> mixture -> test -> edge/multi-person extensions -> observed profiles.
Age prose branches by material, rejoins at Bayesian comparison and confidence intervals, then feeds anomaly and consistency tasks.
The paper closes with usage classification, sensitivity, strengths, and limitations.

language_observations.summary: First/Following/Second/Third/Finally markers expose the summary's model staircase.
However/Therefore moves convert a research gap and wear taxonomy into method selection.
Each bold assumption is immediately followed by a plain-language rationale.
Data Collected/Tool Required/Precautions repeats as a fieldwork information order.
However introduces the discrete-data obstacle before triangulation is selected.
In contrast keeps upward and downward claims parallel under one coordinate axis.
For wooden/For stone branches keep material-specific age evidence distinct.
Once the uncertainty is determined closes derivation and hands a confidence interval to reliability assessment.
If the calculated value falls within an interval turns consistency into an explicit comparison rule.
Strength and weakness bullets separate claimed value from stated boundary at close.

Confirms the full hierarchy and page allocation, including references and AI disclosure.
Maps measurement preparation to two core models, age estimation, further exploration, and evaluation.
Binds symbols, meanings, and units across wear, traffic, C14, weathering, and depth.
Shows the kind of high-poly staircase geometry expected from 3D scanning.
Illustrates the overhead-photo to monocular-depth workflow and scale correction.
Records 11 self-collected samples by location, material, and qualitative wear.
Connects four sampling locations to representative source photographs.
Displays depth heatmaps for three samples used to motivate continuous wear surfaces.
Reports usage time, wear volume, condition, and inferred daily traffic for all 11 samples.
Contrasts force placement when going upstairs and downstairs.
Shows Monte Carlo surfaces and heatmaps for upward, downward, and mixed direction patterns.
Compares measured projection curves classified as mixed, mostly downward, and mostly upward.
Shows multi-peak wear for pairs moving upward and downward.
Compares single-file and double-file projection curves.
Contrasts overlapping mixed two-way traffic with separated left-down/right-up traffic.
Defines three normalized chemical-weathering indices used in the weighted stone-age score.
Illustrates discontinuous versus consistent surface-age distributions for repair detection.
Ranks Model I parameter sensitivity through plotted perturbation responses.
Shows Model II response changes under mu, sigma, and upward-share perturbations.
Confirms references [1]-[14] and the end of authorial paper content.
Separates generated code assistance from author language and formal paper evidence.

judge_relevance_hypotheses.summary: A full task-to-method chain plausibly improves coverage traceability but does not validate the results.
Self-collected samples plausibly signal initiative, while missing calibration limits evidentiary weight.
Explicit limitations plausibly improve credibility because the paper names measurement and trajectory uncertainty.

weaknesses.summary: The claimed non-destructive measurement plan also proposes surface swabbing and portable isotope/mineral analysis without specifying sampling damage, calibration, or cost.
Carbon-14 is described as applicable to stone or construction material in one passage, although the later age model applies it to wood; material scope is inconsistent.
The 11 stair samples are self-collected from photographs, but raw images, camera calibration, depth-model version, ground truth, and uncertainty are not supplied.
Equation (6) omits load P even though the preceding Archard form and later inversion retain P; dimensional consistency is not established.
The prose says formula (1) is reused after simplifying abrasive wear, but formula (1) is the surface-volume integral rather than the Archard relation.
The theoretical values d=0.01 m and P=650 N are applied across all samples without a distribution, source-specific calibration, or sensitivity at that step.
The Bayesian traffic inversion estimates time using wear generated by the same Archard relation and does not show an external age observation or posterior diagnostics.
Equation (14) is called truncated normal but prints an ordinary normal density restricted to y>=0 without a truncation normalization constant.
The Shapiro-Wilk rule is stated for n=10 while the source has 11 stair samples, and its use for a truncated-normal alternative is not justified.
The edge multiplier 1+k_edge|y| has no fitted value, units, coordinate normalization, or validation against edge measurements.
The number of Gaussian peaks is treated as the number of simultaneous walkers, but long-run superposition, changing lanes, and peak identifiability are not tested.
Weathering index notation is inconsistent, weights are left adjustable by rock type, and the exponential decay plus additive microbial beta lacks calibration data.
The age likelihood uses V_obs and V_theory even after the section shifts to chemical weathering, leaving the observed quantity and forward map ambiguous.
Uncertainty propagation assumes independent inputs although W_current, lambda, beta, and weighted chemical indices may be correlated.
Equation (34) defines z from wear depth d_w while the repair narrative says it compares estimated ages; the anomaly variable is inconsistent.
A measured Archard coefficient or chemical composition can narrow a material source but cannot by itself uniquely trace a quarry or wood origin without reference distributions.
The excess-kurtosis thresholds are stated as greater than 3 versus at most 3 even though Equation (41) subtracts 3; raw and excess kurtosis thresholds are conflated.
The sensitivity conclusion says changes have little effect and imply good generalization, but no perturbation range, joint sensitivity, external test, or uncertainty band supports that inference.
Model II sensitivity plots lack raw values, units, response definition, and a reproducible parameter grid.
The AI report supplies generated GLTF processing code, but no evidence shows that the code was executed, validated on the 11 samples, or reconciled with the reported depth pipeline.

independent_extensions.summary: Release calibrated raw images, camera poses, ruler scale, repeat scans, and depth ground truth for the 11 samples.
Restore dimensional consistency in abrasive wear and estimate person-level load and slip distributions rather than fixed constants.
Fit and compare lane-count mixture models with uncertainty instead of equating observed peaks directly to simultaneous people.
Calibrate rock-specific weathering kinetics and correlated chemical indices against dated reference stones.
Run global joint sensitivity and posterior predictive checks on an independently dated staircase.

candidate_rule_impacts.action: retain enumerated task decomposition, fieldwork information order, matched direction contrasts, and confidence-bound handoffs
attach sample images, heatmaps, profiles, tables, and sensitivity plots to explicit analytical purposes
separate self-fit, qualitative pattern match, interval comparison, sensitivity, and external validation
bind camera scale, angle correction, assays, raw point clouds, and sample provenance
test coupled material, time, distribution, weathering, and lane parameters across regimes
retain the AI-disclosure provenance boundary and require generated depth/triangulation code to be executed and reconciled with reported results
attach traffic, direction, age, repair, source, and usage classifications to an evidence grade
